To be a perfect, representative example of something — to have exactly the qualities that people associate most strongly with a particular type, group, era, or idea.

Imagine you're explaining what a "typical villain" looks like to someone who's never seen one. You point to a character who is manipulative, selfish, and cruel — and you say, "He typifies the classic villain."

You're not just saying he's a villain. You're saying: he has all the qualities — the exact features — that most people picture when they imagine that kind of character. He's like a textbook definition brought to life. That's what typify does. It says: this thing perfectly captures the essential nature of that whole category.
How It Works in a Sentence

The structure is simple:

[Something] typifies [a category or quality]

The subject on the left is the specific thing. What comes after typifies is the broader category it represents.

  • "The golden retriever typifies the friendly family dog."
    Of all dogs, the golden retriever most perfectly captures what people picture when they think "friendly family dog."
  • "Her calm, methodical approach typifies the best surgeons."
    Her way of working is so characteristic of great surgeons that she could stand as the model for all of them.
  • "Rainy grey skies typify November in London."
    If you had to sum up London in November, grey rainy skies would be the most defining, characteristic feature.

Notice: in every case, the subject isn't just associated with the category — it captures the very essence of it.

1. A person or thing typifies a category — it's the most representative specimen of that group.

  • "This diner, with its chrome stools and neon signs, typifies American pop culture of the 1950s."
  • "The Labrador typifies what people want in a working dog."

2. A behavior or quality typifies a person, group, or period — it's a reliable, defining feature of them.

  • "This kind of careless mistake typifies his early work." (It's characteristic of how he worked early on.)
  • "Bold, geometric patterns typify the Art Deco style." (They're the most defining visual quality of that style.)

Both uses do the same job: they say something is so characteristic and representative that it captures the essential nature of something else.

It can be positive or negative. The word itself is neutral — it just means "representative."

  • Positive: "Her warmth and generosity typify everything we admire about her."
  • Negative: "This reckless decision typifies the government's poor judgment."

It implies reliability, not coincidence. When you say something typifies X, you're implying this is a recurring, consistent characteristic — not a fluke. It's what you'd expect from that person, group, or thing.

It means representative, not unique. If something typifies a category, others in that category still exist. The golden retriever typifies the friendly family dog, but so can other breeds. Typifying something doesn't mean being the only example.

It does not mean "the best." Typify means being the most characteristic, not necessarily the most exceptional. Something can typify mediocrity just as easily as it can typify excellence.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Exemplify is the closest synonym and can often be swapped in. The subtle difference: exemplify means to be a good, clear example of something. Typify carries a stronger sense of being representative — of having the most defining, characteristic qualities of a category. You might say a speech exemplifies great rhetoric (it's a fine example), but you'd say it typifies the political style of an era (it captures that era's defining qualities).

Epitomize is stronger than typify. It means to be the perfect or ultimate example — the absolute best case of something. Typify is more neutral and grounded — just reliably, characteristically representative.

Embody means to give a concrete, living form to something abstract. "She embodies grace." It's about making the abstract visible and real. Typify is more about being a characteristic specimen of a category rather than giving form to an abstraction.

Characterize often works in the reverse direction. You usually say a quality characterizes something ("Honesty characterizes her work"), describing what defines a subject. With typify, the subject stands as a representative of a wider class ("Her work typifies the best journalism of this decade").

• The golden retriever typifies the friendly family dog. (present, third person)
  • That old diner typified 1950s American culture. (past tense)
  • He spent his career typifying what a great teacher looks like. (ongoing action)
  • He is a man typified by his patience and calm. (passive — he is defined/characterized by these traits)
Final Summary to Lock It In

Typify = to be the most representative, characteristic example of something. When X typifies Y, X doesn't just belong to category Y — X is what Y looks like. It captures Y's defining essence so well that it could serve as the model, the symbol, the textbook case for all of Y.
